# How to read this document

This file is the complete, executable pipeline of the project: it
downloads seven youth-deprivation indicators from the OECD SDG API for
24 European countries, fills residual gaps from Eurostat, cleans and
orients the data, discretises it into ordinal deprivation grades, builds
a partially ordered set (poset) of country profiles, and identifies
which countries fall below a normative acceptability threshold — twice,
with two independent implementations that are cross-checked against each
other.

## Loading the packages

The next chunk loads every package used downstream: `httr` (API
downloads), `readr`/`dplyr`/`tidyr`/`purrr` (data manipulation),
`corrplot`/`pheatmap`/`ggplot2` (figures), `parsec` (the reference R
implementation of poset-based deprivation measurement, by Fattore &
Arcagni), `jsonlite` (final summary export) and `eurostat` (third-source
fallback for permanent OECD data gaps).

```{r setup}
library(httr)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(corrplot)
library(pheatmap)
library(ggplot2)
library(parsec)
library(jsonlite)
library(eurostat)
```

## Countries and indicators

The next chunk declares the sample and the indicator set. The 24
European countries are the project's declared scope (the discretisation
later anchors cut-points to EU policy targets, so a European sample is a
methodological requirement, not a convenience). Raw data is nevertheless
downloaded for all OECD countries, so that exclusions can be verified on
the data at every run instead of assumed. Seven indicators are declared,
each with its SDG series code, age band, and orientation flag
(`invert = TRUE` marks series that measure the *opposite* of deprivation
at the source and must be flipped later).

```{r config}
# the 24 European countries that form the project's declared sample
european_countries <- c("AUT", "BEL", "CHE", "CZE", "DEU", "DNK", "ESP", "EST",
                        "FIN", "FRA", "GBR", "GRC", "HUN", "IRL", "ITA", "LTU",
                        "LVA", "NLD", "NOR", "POL", "PRT", "SVK", "SVN", "SWE")

# all OECD countries: downloaded too, so exclusions are verified, not assumed
all_countries <- c(european_countries, "AUS", "CAN", "CHL", "ISR", "USA",
                   "COL", "CRI", "ISL", "JPN", "KOR", "LUX", "MEX", "NZL", "TUR")

# the seven indicators: SDG goal, series code, age band, orientation.
# invert = TRUE marks "positive" series (they measure who is ABOVE a
# minimum threshold, i.e. the opposite of deprivation)
indicators <- tribble(
  ~name,           ~goal, ~series,                                ~age,     ~invert,
  "poverty",       1,     "1_2_1_OECD",                           "Y18T25", FALSE,
  "neet",          8,     "8_6_1_SL_TLF_NEET_19ICLS",             "Y15T24", FALSE,
  "unemp",         8,     "8_5_2_SL_TLF_UEM_19ICLS",              "Y15T24", FALSE,
  "skill_math",    4,     "4_1_1_SE_TOT_PRFL_LOWSEC_SKILL_MATH",  "_T",     TRUE,
  "skill_read",    4,     "4_1_1_SE_TOT_PRFL_LOWSEC_SKILL_READ",  "_T",     TRUE,
  "early_leaving", 4,     "4_1_2_SE_TOT_CPLR_UPPSEC",             "_T",     TRUE,
  "bank_acct",     8,     "8_10_2_FB_BNK_ACCSS",                  "Y15T24", TRUE
)
```

*Result and decisions.* Four decisions about this indicator set were
taken before any analysis, and are recorded here because they shape
everything downstream. (1) `unemp` is included even though it overlaps
definitionally with `neet` (every unemployed young person not in
education is also NEET); whether the overlap is empirically excessive is
decided later, in the cleaning step, from the data. (2) `early_leaving`
is **not** what its name suggests: the EU "early school leavers, 18–24"
indicator is a Eurostat structural indicator and does not exist in the
UN SDG framework this API exposes. The closest series is SDG 4.1.2, the
*upper-secondary completion rate*; it is used inverted, as a proxy, and
renamed `low_completion` after inversion so the name never overclaims.
Its `AGE = "_T"` is the series' own design (SDG completion indicators
define their reference ages internally), not a mixing of all ages. (3) A
mortality indicator (Goal 3) was attempted and dropped: two rounds of
live API queries showed no youth-specific mortality series exists in
this dataset, and every available proxy either broke the 15–24 framing
or measured a different concept. Goal 3 is out rather than patched. (4)
`skill_read` and `bank_acct` are downloaded but provisionally: the
cleaning step decides their fate.

## Downloading the raw data

The next chunk downloads the raw data, one SDG goal at a time (goals 1,
4, 8), from the OECD SDMX REST API, with three retries per call and a
4-second pause between goals (the OECD rate limit is 20 requests per
minute). Each goal is downloaded once even if several indicators use it.

```{r download}
download_goal <- function(goal) {
  # the API wants countries sorted and joined with "+"; the 10 empty
  # SDMX dimensions mean "all series, all ages, all sexes"
  country_key <- paste(sort(all_countries), collapse = "+")
  key <- paste0(country_key, strrep(".", 10))
  url <- paste0(
    "https://sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/OECD.WISE.RSB,DSD_SDG@DF_SDG_G_",
    goal, ",2.0/", key,
    "?format=csvfilewithlabels&dimensionAtObservation=AllDimensions",
    "&startPeriod=2013&endPeriod=2025"
  )
  for (attempt in 1:3) {
    response <- GET(url, timeout(120))
    if (status_code(response) == 200) break
    Sys.sleep(5)   # transient overload: wait and retry
  }
  stopifnot(status_code(response) == 200)
  read_csv(content(response, "text", encoding = "UTF-8"), show_col_types = FALSE)
}

raw_data_by_goal <- list()
for (goal in unique(indicators$goal)) {
  raw_data_by_goal[[as.character(goal)]] <- download_goal(goal)
  Sys.sleep(4)   # respect the 20-requests-per-minute rate limit
}
```

*Result.* Three raw tables (goals 1, 4, 8), 2013–2025, all OECD
countries, all series. Nothing is filtered yet: filtering happens per
indicator in the next chunk, and any failure there can be diagnosed
against the full raw download.

## Extracting one indicator at a time

The next chunk filters each indicator out of its goal's raw table using
SDMX dimension *codes* (`SDG_SERIES`, `AGE`, `SEX`), never text labels.
A diagnostic helper prints what is actually available whenever a
(series, age, sex) combination returns zero rows — the pipeline is built
to fail loudly with actionable output rather than continue with an empty
table. The two PISA series are restricted to actual PISA cycle years
(2015, 2018, 2022), because the 4.1.1 dataflow mixes in non-PISA
observations that are not comparable across countries.

```{r filter}
extract_indicator <- function(raw_data, series, age, sex = "_T") {
  raw_data %>%
    filter(SDG_SERIES == series) %>%
    filter(AGE == age) %>%
    filter(SEX == sex) %>%
    select(iso3 = REF_AREA, year = TIME_PERIOD, value = OBS_VALUE) %>%
    mutate(year = as.integer(year), value = as.numeric(value)) %>%
    # if other breakdowns leave duplicates, keep one declared row rather
    # than accidentally summing or averaging
    distinct(iso3, year, .keep_all = TRUE)
}

# diagnostic: when a combination returns 0 rows, print what IS available
diagnose_empty <- function(raw_data, series, age, goal, name, sex = "_T") {
  series_in_goal <- sort(unique(raw_data$SDG_SERIES))
  series_exists <- series %in% series_in_goal
  cat(sprintf("\n[%s] series '%s' / AGE = '%s' / SEX = '%s' returned 0 rows (goal %s).\n",
              name, series, age, sex, goal))
  if (!series_exists) {
    prefix <- sub("^([0-9]+_[0-9A-Za-z]+_[0-9]+).*", "\\1", series)
    close_matches <- grep(paste0("^", prefix), series_in_goal, value = TRUE)
    cat("  Series code not found among the", length(series_in_goal),
        "series downloaded for goal", goal, ".\n")
    if (length(close_matches) > 0) {
      cat("  Series sharing the same SDG code prefix ('", prefix, "'):\n", sep = "")
      print(close_matches)
    } else {
      cat("  All series available for this goal:\n")
      print(series_in_goal)
    }
  } else {
    series_rows <- raw_data %>% filter(SDG_SERIES == series)
    cat("  Series exists, but not for AGE = '", age, "' / SEX = '", sex, "'.\n", sep = "")
    cat("  AGE codes available:\n"); print(sort(unique(series_rows$AGE)))
    cat("  SEX codes available:\n"); print(sort(unique(series_rows$SEX)))
  }
  invisible(series_exists)
}

all_indicators_data <- list()
for (i in 1:nrow(indicators)) {
  current_indicator <- indicators[i, ]
  raw <- raw_data_by_goal[[as.character(current_indicator$goal)]]
  df <- extract_indicator(raw, current_indicator$series, current_indicator$age)
  if (nrow(df) == 0) {
    diagnose_empty(raw, current_indicator$series, current_indicator$age,
                   current_indicator$goal, current_indicator$name)
  }
  # PISA series: keep only real PISA cycles, other years are not comparable
  if (current_indicator$name %in% c("skill_math", "skill_read")) {
    df <- df %>% filter(year %in% c(2015, 2018, 2022))
  }
  df$indicator <- current_indicator$name
  all_indicators_data[[i]] <- df
}

long_data <- bind_rows(all_indicators_data)

# hard check: every declared indicator must have produced rows
missing_series <- setdiff(indicators$name, unique(long_data$indicator))
if (length(missing_series) > 0) {
  stop("No data downloaded for: ", paste(missing_series, collapse = ", "),
       " — see the diagnostic output above, then fix the `indicators` table.")
}
```

## Eurostat fallback for permanent OECD gaps

Some cells are missing from the OECD data in *every* year, not just
recent ones. For four indicators a genuine Eurostat equivalent exists
and is used as a third, last-resort source before a country is dropped:
`neet` (`edat_lfse_20`), `unemp` (`une_rt_a`), `early_leaving`
(`edat_lfse_14`), `poverty` (`ilc_li02`). The exact filter codes below
were verified against live data (Italy 2024 values cross-checked against
published figures), not guessed from documentation. `skill_math`,
`skill_read` and `bank_acct` have no Eurostat equivalent (PISA and
Global Findex are not replicated by Eurostat) and are excluded from the
fallback on purpose.

**Orientation warning — this is where the corrected bug originates.**
Every Eurostat fallback series measures deprivation *directly* (share of
NEET, share unemployed, share of early leavers, share at risk of
poverty). The OECD series for `early_leaving`, however, is a
*completion* rate, i.e. positively oriented, and the `{r orient}` chunk
later inverts that whole column. A raw Eurostat early-leavers value
dropped into that column would therefore be inverted *by mistake*. The
`deprivation_oriented` flag added below lets the gap-filling step store
such values pre-compensated (as `100 - value`), so the later uniform
inversion restores them to their true meaning. For `neet`, `unemp` and
`poverty` the OECD and Eurostat orientations agree and no compensation
is needed.

```{r eurostat-setup}
# Eurostat geo codes are ISO2 with two exceptions: Greece "EL", UK "UK"
eurostat_geo_map <- c(
  AUT = "AT", BEL = "BE", CHE = "CH", CZE = "CZ", DEU = "DE", DNK = "DK",
  ESP = "ES", EST = "EE", FIN = "FI", FRA = "FR", GBR = "UK", GRC = "EL",
  HUN = "HU", IRL = "IE", ITA = "IT", LTU = "LT", LVA = "LV", NLD = "NL",
  NOR = "NO", POL = "PL", PRT = "PT", SVK = "SK", SVN = "SI", SWE = "SE"
)

# dataset IDs + verified filter codes. deprivation_oriented = TRUE means
# the Eurostat series already measures deprivation directly (all four do)
eurostat_dataset_map <- list(
  neet = list(id = "edat_lfse_20",
              filters = list(age = "Y15-24", training = "NO_FE_NO_NFE",
                             wstatus = "NEMP"),
              deprivation_oriented = TRUE),   # NEET rate, Italy 2024 = 12.0%
  unemp = list(id = "une_rt_a",
               filters = list(age = "Y15-24", unit = "PC_ACT"),
               deprivation_oriented = TRUE),  # unemployment rate, Italy 2024 = 20.3%
  early_leaving = list(id = "edat_lfse_14",
                       filters = list(age = "Y18-24", wstatus = "POP"),
                       deprivation_oriented = TRUE), # EARLY LEAVERS share, Italy 2024 = 9.8%
                       # NOTE: opposite orientation vs the OECD completion series!
  poverty = list(id = "ilc_li02",
                 filters = list(age = "Y18-24", unit = "PC",
                                indic_il = "LI_R_MD60"),
                 deprivation_oriented = TRUE) # AROP 60% median, Italy 2024 = 20.9%
  # skill_math, skill_read, bank_acct: no Eurostat equivalent, not attempted
)

# resolve one (indicator, country) gap via Eurostat; NULL on failure,
# printing exactly why (the same diagnose-first pattern as the OECD side)
try_eurostat <- function(ind_name, ctry_iso3) {
  if (!(ind_name %in% names(eurostat_dataset_map))) {
    cat(sprintf("  No Eurostat equivalent registered for '%s' — skipping.\n", ind_name))
    return(NULL)
  }
  geo_code <- eurostat_geo_map[[ctry_iso3]]
  if (is.null(geo_code) || is.na(geo_code)) {
    cat(sprintf("  No Eurostat geo code known for '%s' — skipping.\n", ctry_iso3))
    return(NULL)
  }
  spec <- eurostat_dataset_map[[ind_name]]
  all_filters <- c(list(geo = geo_code), spec$filters)

  raw_eu <- tryCatch(
    eurostat::get_eurostat(spec$id, filters = all_filters, time_format = "num"),
    error = function(e) {
      cat(sprintf("  Eurostat download failed for %s / %s: %s\n",
                  spec$id, ctry_iso3, conditionMessage(e)))
      NULL
    }
  )
  if (is.null(raw_eu) || nrow(raw_eu) == 0) {
    cat(sprintf("  Eurostat dataset %s returned no rows for %s.\n", spec$id, ctry_iso3))
    return(NULL)
  }
  if ("TIME_PERIOD" %in% names(raw_eu) && !("time" %in% names(raw_eu))) {
    raw_eu <- raw_eu %>% rename(time = TIME_PERIOD)
  }
  if ("sex" %in% names(raw_eu)) raw_eu <- raw_eu %>% filter(sex == "T")

  # cap at 2024: Eurostat sometimes carries provisional current-year data
  # that would silently sit one year ahead of every other cell
  raw_eu <- raw_eu %>% filter(time <= 2024)
  if (nrow(raw_eu) == 0) {
    cat(sprintf("  %s / %s: no Eurostat data at or before 2024.\n", spec$id, ctry_iso3))
    return(NULL)
  }

  # safety net: with the verified filters exactly one row per year should
  # remain; if not, print everything and give up rather than guess
  per_year <- raw_eu %>% count(time)
  if (any(per_year$n > 1)) {
    cat(sprintf("  UNEXPECTED AMBIGUITY: %s / %s has multiple rows per year — printing all:\n",
                spec$id, ctry_iso3))
    print(raw_eu)
    return(NULL)
  }

  best <- raw_eu %>% filter(!is.na(values)) %>% filter(time == max(time))
  if (nrow(best) != 1) {
    cat(sprintf("  %s / %s: no non-NA value in any year.\n", spec$id, ctry_iso3))
    return(NULL)
  }
  list(value = best$values[1], year = best$time[1],
       deprivation_oriented = isTRUE(spec$deprivation_oriented))
}
```

## From time series to a per-country matrix

The next chunk collapses the time dimension to a cross-section (latest
available year per country–indicator inside the primary 2019–2024 wind;
(2) widened OECD window 2015–2024 — bounded, not "any year ever"; (3)
Eurostat equivalent series, where one exists; (4) drop the country —
last resort. Every step prints what it does, cell by cell, and writes to
persistent logs that end in the final summary.

**The corrected orientation handling is here.** When a cell is filled
from Eurostat *and* the OECD column it lands in is scheduled for
inversion in `{r orient}` (`invert = TRUE` in the `indicators` table),
the Eurostat value — already deprivation-oriented — is stored as
`100 - value`, so that the later uniform inversion restores it.

```{r cross-section}
# primary rule: latest available year within 2019-2024
windowed_data <- long_data %>% filter(year >= 2019, year <= 2024)
latest_data <- windowed_data %>%
  group_by(iso3, indicator) %>%
  filter(year == max(year)) %>%
  ungroup()

country_matrix <- latest_data %>%
  select(iso3, indicator, value) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicator, values_from = value)

# print who is incomplete across the FULL sample (verify, don't assume)
incomplete_countries <- country_matrix %>%
  filter(if_any(everything(), is.na)) %>%
  pull(iso3)
cat("Countries with incomplete data in the 2019-2024 window: ",
    if (length(incomplete_countries) > 0) paste(incomplete_countries, collapse = ", ") else "none",
    "\n", sep = "")

europe_matrix <- country_matrix %>% filter(iso3 %in% european_countries)

gap_cells <- which(is.na(as.matrix(europe_matrix %>% select(-iso3))), arr.ind = TRUE)

widen_log <- character(0)
eurostat_fallback_log <- character(0)

if (nrow(gap_cells) > 0) {
  ind_names <- names(europe_matrix)[-1]
  cat(sprintf("\nSearching for %d European country-indicator gap(s) in 2019-2024:\n",
              nrow(gap_cells)))
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(gap_cells))) {
    ctry <- europe_matrix$iso3[gap_cells[k, "row"]]
    ind  <- ind_names[gap_cells[k, "col"]]

    # step 2: widen to 2015-2024 (bounded widening)
    candidates <- long_data %>%
      filter(iso3 == ctry, indicator == ind, year >= 2015, year <= 2024)
    if (nrow(candidates) > 0) {
      best <- candidates %>% filter(year == max(year))
      cat(sprintf("  WIDENED: %s / %s -> using year %d (outside 2019-2024, within 2015-2024)\n",
                  ctry, ind, best$year[1]))
      europe_matrix[europe_matrix$iso3 == ctry, ind] <- best$value[1]
      widen_log <- c(widen_log, sprintf("%s/%s: year %d (OECD, widened)", ctry, ind, best$year[1]))
    } else {
      # step 3: try Eurostat before giving up on the cell
      cat(sprintf("  STILL MISSING in OECD data (2015-2024): %s / %s -> trying Eurostat...\n",
                  ctry, ind))
      eu_result <- try_eurostat(ind, ctry)
      if (!is.null(eu_result)) {
        # ORIENTATION FIX: if this column will be inverted later (the OECD
        # series is positively oriented) but the Eurostat series already
        # measures deprivation, store 100 - value so the later inversion
        # restores the true value instead of corrupting it
        will_be_inverted <- indicators$invert[indicators$name == ind]
        value_to_store <- if (will_be_inverted && eu_result$deprivation_oriented) {
          cat(sprintf("  ORIENTATION FIX: %s / %s: Eurostat value %.2f is deprivation-oriented, OECD column is completion-oriented -> storing %.2f (= 100 - value) so {r orient} restores it\n",
                      ctry, ind, eu_result$value, 100 - eu_result$value))
          100 - eu_result$value
        } else {
          eu_result$value
        }
        cat(sprintf("  EUROSTAT: %s / %s -> year %d, value %.2f (dataset %s — NOT the OECD series: check comparability)\n",
                    ctry, ind, eu_result$year, eu_result$value,
                    eurostat_dataset_map[[ind]]$id))
        europe_matrix[europe_matrix$iso3 == ctry, ind] <- value_to_store
        eurostat_fallback_log <- c(eurostat_fallback_log,
                                   sprintf("%s/%s: year %d, dataset %s, raw value %.2f%s",
                                           ctry, ind, eu_result$year,
                                           eurostat_dataset_map[[ind]]$id,
                                           eu_result$value,
                                           if (will_be_inverted && eu_result$deprivation_oriented)
                                             " (stored pre-compensated for inversion)" else ""))
      } else {
        cat(sprintf("  STILL MISSING: %s / %s -> no usable data anywhere. Country will be dropped.\n",
                    ctry, ind))
      }
    }
  }
} else {
  cat("\nNo widening needed: every European country has data in 2019-2024.\n")
}

# drop European countries still incomplete after all three sources
country_removal_log <- character(0)
incomplete_europe <- europe_matrix %>% filter(if_any(-iso3, is.na))
if (nrow(incomplete_europe) > 0) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(incomplete_europe))) {
    ctry <- incomplete_europe$iso3[i]
    row_flags <- is.na(as.matrix(incomplete_europe[i, -1, drop = FALSE]))
    missing_inds <- names(incomplete_europe)[-1][as.vector(row_flags)]
    cat(sprintf("DROPPED %s: no usable data anywhere for: %s\n",
                ctry, paste(missing_inds, collapse = ", ")))
    country_removal_log <- c(country_removal_log,
                             sprintf("%s: missing %s", ctry, paste(missing_inds, collapse = ", ")))
  }
  europe_matrix <- europe_matrix %>% filter(!iso3 %in% incomplete_europe$iso3)
} else {
  cat("No European country dropped: all complete after the search.\n")
}

n_countries <- nrow(europe_matrix)
cat(sprintf("\nFinal European sample: %d countries (out of %d listed)\n",
            n_countries, length(european_countries)))
```

*Result and decisions.* On the reference run exactly four gaps survived
the widened OECD search, all on `early_leaving` (the OECD completion
series has no data at all for CZE, IRL, NLD, SVK), and all four were
resolved from Eurostat `edat_lfse_14`, year 2024, with the orientation
fix applied (raw early-leaver shares: CZE 5.4, IRL 2.8, NLD 7.0, SVK
7.5). No cell needed the widened OECD window, and no country was
dropped: the final sample is the full 24. Caveat, declared rather than
hidden: those four cells measure the *EU early-leaver concept* (18–24,
at most lower-secondary attainment, not in education), while the other
20 cells of that column measure *non-completion of upper secondary* —
conceptually adjacent but not identical, and the early-leaver measure is
systematically lower. The four substituted countries are all well below
every cut-point on this dimension, so their grade (0) is robust to this
mismatch, but the mismatch itself is real and is carried into the limits
section of the report.

## Orienting the indicators

The next chunk flips the four positively-oriented series (`100 - value`)
so that in the final matrix **higher always means more deprivation**,
and renames them so each name states what the column measures *after*
inversion (`skill_math` becomes `lowskill_math`, `early_leaving` becomes
`low_completion`, etc.).

```{r orient}
oriented_matrix <- europe_matrix %>%
  mutate(
    skill_math    = 100 - skill_math,
    skill_read    = 100 - skill_read,
    bank_acct     = 100 - bank_acct,
    early_leaving = 100 - early_leaving
  ) %>%
  rename(lowskill_math  = skill_math,
         lowskill_read  = skill_read,
         no_bank_acct   = bank_acct,
         low_completion = early_leaving)

stopifnot(nrow(oriented_matrix) == n_countries)
stopifnot(!any(is.na(select(oriented_matrix, -iso3))))
cat(sprintf("Matrix before cleaning: %d x %d indicators\n",
            n_countries, ncol(oriented_matrix) - 1))
```
## Automatic cleaning step

Two removals of two different kinds happen next. Rule (1) is
**pre-registered** (decided before looking at results): drop
`no_bank_acct` if it is nearly saturated across Europe (financial
inclusion in advanced economies approaches 96–99% per the World Bank
Global Findex 2021, so the indicator may not discriminate). Step (2) is
**not pre-registered and is flagged as such**: the full pairwise
Spearman correlation matrix of the surviving indicators is plotted
first, and `lowskill_read` and `no_bank_acct` are then removed manually,
based on what the matrix shows. This is a weaker standard than rule (1)
— a post-hoc pick, declared plainly instead of dressed up as a rule.
Everything removed is logged with its reason.

```{r auto-clean, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5.5}
removal_log <- character(0)

# --- 1. pre-registered: drop no_bank_acct if nearly saturated ---
# threshold scales with n_countries so it keeps meaning ~5/8 of the sample
near_zero_bank_threshold <- ceiling(15 / 24 * n_countries)
n_near_zero_bank <- sum(oriented_matrix$no_bank_acct < 2, na.rm = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Countries with no_bank_acct < 2%%: %d / %d (threshold: %d)\n",
            n_near_zero_bank, n_countries, near_zero_bank_threshold))
if (n_near_zero_bank >= near_zero_bank_threshold) {
  cat(sprintf("REMOVED no_bank_acct: %d/%d countries below 2%% (near-saturation).\n",
              n_near_zero_bank, n_countries))
  oriented_matrix <- oriented_matrix %>% select(-no_bank_acct)
  removal_log <- c(removal_log,
                   sprintf("no_bank_acct: saturation (%d/%d countries < 2%%)",
                           n_near_zero_bank, n_countries))
}

# --- 2. NOT pre-registered: inspect the full matrix, then decide ---
rho_threshold <- 0.6
surviving <- setdiff(names(oriented_matrix), "iso3")

cor_mat_before <- cor(oriented_matrix %>% select(all_of(surviving)),
                      method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
cat("\nFull pairwise Spearman correlation matrix:\n")
print(round(cor_mat_before, 2))
corrplot(cor_mat_before, method = "color", type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black", number.cex = 0.8,
         tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45,
         title = "Spearman correlation - all indicators",
         mar = c(0, 0, 1, 0))

# manual removal, decided AFTER inspecting the matrix above (post-hoc,
# flagged as such); intersect() guards against already-removed columns
to_drop_manual <- intersect(c("lowskill_read", "no_bank_acct"), surviving)
if (length(to_drop_manual) > 0) {
  cat("REMOVED (manual, post-hoc decision after inspecting the matrix):",
      paste(to_drop_manual, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  removal_log <- c(removal_log,
                   sprintf("%s: removed manually after inspecting the correlation matrix (post-hoc)",
                           to_drop_manual))
  oriented_matrix <- oriented_matrix %>% select(-all_of(to_drop_manual))
  surviving <- setdiff(surviving, to_drop_manual)
}

# re-plot after removal. NOTE: a manual pick does NOT guarantee every
# remaining pair sits below rho_threshold — nothing enforces that here
if (length(surviving) >= 2) {
  cor_mat_after <- cor(oriented_matrix %>% select(all_of(surviving)),
                       method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
  print(round(cor_mat_after, 2))
  corrplot(cor_mat_after, method = "color", type = "upper",
           addCoef.col = "black", number.cex = 0.8,
           tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45,
           title = "Spearman correlation - remaining indicators",
           mar = c(0, 0, 1, 0))
}

final_indicators <- setdiff(names(oriented_matrix), "iso3")
n_dims <- length(final_indicators)
cat(sprintf("\nIndicators after cleaning: %d\n", n_dims))
cat(paste(final_indicators, collapse = ", "), "\n")

write_csv(oriented_matrix, "idea5_matrix_oriented_R.csv")
```

*Result and decisions.* Five indicators survive: `poverty`, `neet`,
`unemp`, `lowskill_math`, `low_completion`. `lowskill_read` was removed
because it tracks `lowskill_math` closely enough to add little
independent information; `no_bank_acct` because in Europe it separates
only a small Mediterranean tail. Both removals are the manual, post-hoc
kind and the log says so — a deliberate weakening of the
pre-registration standard used elsewhere, on explicit request, declared
rather than disguised. `unemp`, whose overlap with `neet` motivated its
removal in an earlier six-indicator version, stays: on this sample their
correlation (0.42) is below the 0.6 bar.

## Exploratory analysis: why a poset at all

The empirical premise of the whole project: if the surviving indicators
were strongly correlated, a plain average would lose almost nothing and
the poset machinery would be unjustified. The next chunks compute
summary statistics, a boxplot, a value heatmap, the full Spearman
correlation matrix, and the best/worst country per indicator.

*Result.* On the corrected matrix the median absolute Spearman
correlation is **0.27**; the strongest pair is poverty–low_completion
(0.57), still below the 0.6 bar. Maxima of deprivation are scattered —
Norway worst on poverty, Lithuania on NEET, Greece on unemployment and
mathematics, Denmark on non-completion; Ireland is best on poverty and

everywhere: the dimensions carry genuinely different information, which

## Ordinal discretisation

Each indicator is mapped to three deprivation grades (0 = low, 1 =
medium, 2 = high). The placement of the cut-points is the most
attackable choice of the whole project, so it is made twice, with two
schemes whose comparison is itself a result.

**Schema A (main) — policy-anchored cut-points, with three declared
levels of anchoring.** Each threshold is one of: an **official EU
target** (institutional objective at EU level), an **empirical anchor**
(calibrated on EU averages or baselines), or a **normative convention**
(the author's declared choice, guided by the literature). Indicator by
indicator:

-   **NEET** — 9 [official EU target]: the European Pillar of Social
    Rights Action Plan (COM(2021) 102 final, adopted at the Porto Social
    Summit 2021) targets a NEET rate (15–29) below 9% by 2030. 12
    [empirical anchor]: the pre-pandemic 2019 EU baseline (12.6%) that
    the same Action Plan names as the critical starting level. The
    indicator here covers 15–24 rather than 15–29; the Council
    Recommendation on the reinforced Youth Guarantee (2020/C 372/01)
    confirms 15–24 as the historical core of EU youth policy, and the
    mismatch is declared.
-   **Low achievers in mathematics (PISA)** — 15 [official EU target]:
    the Council Resolution on the European Education Area strategic
    framework (2021/C 66/01) targets fewer than 15% low-achieving
    15-year-olds by 2030. 30 [normative convention / empirical anchor]:
    twice the official target, clearly above the post-PISA-2022 EU
    average (\~22.9%, OECD PISA 2022 Results), marking severe
    educational distress.
-   **Youth poverty (AROP)** — no official EU percentage target exists
    (the EPSR poverty target is absolute: −15 million AROPE persons), so
    both cuts are anchored differently. 20 [empirical anchor]: the EU
    average at-risk-of-poverty rate for young people (15–29) is \~19.3%
    (Eurostat, EU-SILC). 10 [normative convention]: about half the EU
    average, isolating best performers. Declared caveat: the OECD series
    used here follows the OECD 50%-of-median convention while the
    Eurostat AROP statistic is 60%-of-median, so the empirical anchor is
    approximate and conservative.
-   **Youth unemployment** — the EPSR sets no isolated
    youth-unemployment target. 20 [empirical anchor]: clearly above the
    EU 15–24 average (\~14.5% in 2023, Eurostat EU-LFS), typical of
    structurally critical labour markets. 10 [normative convention]:
    below the EU average, isolating stable youth labour markets.
-   **Low completion** — 9 and 15 [normative convention]: the lower cut
    borrows the EU early-leavers target (\<9%, EPSR/EEA framework) as
    the nearest institutional anchor. Declared limit, kept deliberately:
    the measured concept (100 − upper-secondary completion) is
    systematically larger than the EU early-leaver share, so these cuts
    are *stricter* in practice than the target they borrow from —
    several well-performing countries land in grade 1–2 on this
    dimension. This is a conscious, declared choice, not an oversight.
-   **No bank account** (removed in cleaning, cuts kept for
    completeness) — 5 [empirical anchor]: World Bank Global Findex 2021
    shows 96–99% account access in advanced economies, so \>5% unbanked
    marks an anomalous friction (coherent with World Bank UFA2020 and UN
    SDG 8.10); 10 [normative convention]: twice the residual
    physiological level.

**Schema B (robustness)** uses terciles of the observed distribution —
purely relative, no policy content: "worse than European peers" instead
of "short of EU targets".

```{r schema-a}
# cut-points for all SEVEN pre-cleaning indicators; the filter below
# keeps only the survivors. Anchoring per cut is documented above.
cuts_a <- tribble(
  ~indicator,      ~cut_low, ~cut_high,
  "poverty",        10,       20,   # normative / EU youth AROP mean ~19.3%
  "neet",           9,        12,   # EPSR Action Plan target / 2019 EU baseline
  "unemp",          10,       20,   # normative / above EU youth mean ~14.5%
  "lowskill_math",  15,       30,   # EEA Council Resolution target / 2x target
  "lowskill_read",  15,       30,   # same anchors as math (removed in cleaning)
  "low_completion", 9,        15,   # EU early-leaver target borrowed as proxy anchor
  "no_bank_acct",   5,        10    # Findex saturation / 2x (removed in cleaning)
)

cuts_a <- cuts_a %>% filter(indicator %in% final_indicators)
stopifnot(setequal(cuts_a$indicator, final_indicators))

discretize_policy <- function(values, cut_low, cut_high) {
  case_when(
    values > cut_high ~ 2,
    values > cut_low  ~ 1,
    TRUE              ~ 0
  )
}

grades_a <- oriented_matrix
for (i in 1:nrow(cuts_a)) {
  cut_row <- cuts_a[i, ]
  grades_a[[cut_row$indicator]] <- discretize_policy(
    oriented_matrix[[cut_row$indicator]], cut_row$cut_low, cut_row$cut_high
  )
}
```

*Result.* Grade counts per indicator are printed two chunks below. Two
facts worth noting now: only **Estonia** (14.97) meets the EU 15%
low-achievers target in mathematics, and on `lowskill_math` 20 of 24
countries sit in the medium band — the EU-level target is demanding for
nearly everyone.

```{r schema-b}
discretize_terciles <- function(values) {
  breakpoints <- quantile(values, probs = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1), na.rm = TRUE)
  breakpoints <- unique(breakpoints)   # merge duplicated breakpoints
  as.integer(cut(values, breaks = breakpoints, include.lowest = TRUE,
                 labels = FALSE)) - 1
}
grades_b <- oriented_matrix %>%
  mutate(across(-iso3, discretize_terciles))
```

```{r discretisation-check}
count_grades <- function(grades_df) {
  grades_df %>%
    select(-iso3) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "indicator", values_to = "grade") %>%
    count(indicator, grade) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = grade, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
}
cat("Grade counts, Schema A (policy):\n");   print(count_grades(grades_a))
cat("\nGrade counts, Schema B (terciles):\n"); print(count_grades(grades_b))

cat("\nCountries meeting the EU low-achievers target (lowskill_math grade 0):\n")
print(grades_a$iso3[grades_a$lowskill_math == 0])

write_csv(grades_a, "idea5_grades_A_R.csv")
write_csv(grades_b, "idea5_grades_B_R.csv")
```

*Result (reference run, Schema A).* poverty 9/12/3, neet 13/6/5, unemp
5/14/5, lowskill_math 1/20/3, low_completion 11/6/7 (grades 0/1/2
respectively). Every grade class is populated for every indicator, so no
dimension is degenerate.

## From-scratch poset toolbox

The analysis is deliberately run twice: once with the from-scratch
implementation below (profile construction, component-wise dominance,
transitive reduction, Bubley–Dyer adjacent-transposition sampling of
linear extensions — the same Markov chain `parsec` uses), and once with
`parsec` itself. If the scratch code is right, the two identification
vectors must be nearly identical; the cross-check happens further down.

```{r scratch-implementation}
# collapse rows sharing the same grade vector into distinct profiles
distinct_profiles <- function(grades) {
  key <- apply(grades, 1, paste, collapse = "")
  uk <- unique(key)
  profiles <- do.call(rbind, lapply(uk, function(k)
    as.integer(strsplit(k, "")[[1]])))
  members <- lapply(uk, function(k) rownames(grades)[key == k])
  list(profiles = profiles, members = members)
}

# leq[i, j] TRUE when profile i <= profile j on EVERY dimension
leq_matrix <- function(profiles) {
  m <- nrow(profiles)
  leq <- matrix(FALSE, m, m)
  for (i in seq_len(m)) for (j in seq_len(m))
    leq[i, j] <- all(profiles[i, ] <= profiles[j, ])
  leq
}

# transitive reduction: the cover pairs = edges of the Hasse diagram
cover_relation <- function(leq) {
  m <- nrow(leq)
  strict <- leq & !diag(m)
  out <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(m)) for (j in seq_len(m))
    if (strict[i, j] && !any(strict[i, ] & strict[, j]))
      out[[length(out) + 1]] <- c(i, j)
  do.call(rbind, out)
}

# depth = length of the longest chain strictly below each node
node_depths <- function(strict) {
  m <- nrow(strict)
  depth <- rep(0L, m)
  for (pass in seq_len(m)) for (i in seq_len(m)) {
    below <- which(strict[, i])
    if (length(below)) depth[i] <- 1L + max(depth[below])
  }
  depth
}

# topological sort: the Bubley-Dyer chain must start from a valid extension
topo_sort <- function(strict) {
  m <- nrow(strict)
  indeg <- as.integer(colSums(strict))
  avail <- which(indeg == 0L)
  out <- integer(0)
  while (length(avail)) {
    x <- avail[length(avail)]
    avail <- avail[-length(avail)]
    out <- c(out, x)
    for (j in which(strict[x, ])) {
      indeg[j] <- indeg[j] - 1L
      if (indeg[j] == 0L) avail <- c(avail, j)
    }
  }
  stopifnot(length(out) == m)   # otherwise not a partial order
  out
}

# Bubley-Dyer sampler: random adjacent transpositions, kept only when
# they do not violate the partial order; returns one row of ranks per sample
sample_les <- function(leq, n_samples, burn_in, thin, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  m <- nrow(leq)
  strict <- leq & !diag(m)
  seqv <- topo_sort(strict)
  total <- burn_in + n_samples * thin
  pos <- sample.int(m - 1, total, replace = TRUE)
  coin <- runif(total) < 0.5
  ranks <- matrix(0L, n_samples, m)
  s <- 0L
  for (t in seq_len(total)) {
    if (coin[t]) {
      i <- pos[t]
      a <- seqv[i]; b <- seqv[i + 1]
      if (!strict[a, b]) { seqv[i] <- b; seqv[i + 1] <- a }
    }
    if (t > burn_in && (t - burn_in) %% thin == 0L) {
      s <- s + 1L
      ranks[s, seqv] <- 0:(m - 1)
    }
  }
  ranks
}

# full evaluation: profiles + tau, sample extensions, per unit compute
# identification (share of extensions ranking it ABOVE tau), severity
# (mean normalised rank gap above tau) and average rank.
# Convention: a unit exactly AT tau counts as deprived (idn = 1)
evaluate_scratch <- function(grades, tau,
                             n_samples = 20000, burn_in = 5000,
                             thin = 5, seed = 42) {
  dp <- distinct_profiles(grades)
  profiles <- dp$profiles
  members <- dp$members
  hit <- which(apply(profiles, 1, function(p) all(p == tau)))
  if (length(hit) == 0) {
    profiles <- rbind(profiles, tau)
    members <- c(members, list("_TAU_"))
    tau_idx <- nrow(profiles)
  } else tau_idx <- hit[1]
  leq <- leq_matrix(profiles)
  ranks <- sample_les(leq, n_samples, burn_in, thin, seed)
  m <- nrow(profiles)
  idn <- colMeans(ranks > ranks[, tau_idx])
  sev <- colMeans(pmax(ranks - ranks[, tau_idx], 0)) / (m - 1)
  avg_rank <- colMeans(ranks)
  idn[tau_idx] <- 1
  rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(members), function(i) {
    mem <- setdiff(members[[i]], "_TAU_")
    if (length(mem) == 0) return(NULL)
    data.frame(unit = mem, idn = idn[i], severity = sev[i],
               avg_rank = avg_rank[i])
  }))
  rows <- rows[match(rownames(grades), rows$unit), ]
  rownames(rows) <- rows$unit
  rows[, c("idn", "severity", "avg_rank")]
}

# share of country pairs whose profiles are incomparable
incomparable_share <- function(grades) {
  v <- as.matrix(grades)
  n <- nrow(v)
  inc <- 0L
  for (i in 1:(n - 1)) for (j in (i + 1):n)
    if (!(all(v[i, ] <= v[j, ]) || all(v[i, ] >= v[j, ]))) inc <- inc + 1L
  inc / (n * (n - 1) / 2)
}
```

*Result.* A self-contained toolbox; nothing has touched the real data
yet. Its correctness is established next, on posets with exactly known
answers.

The next chunk validates the sampler on two tiny posets where the answer
is known exactly: a "V" poset (a \< c, b \< c — a must precede b in
exactly half of all extensions, c is always last) and a 3-element
antichain (all ranks uniform).

```{r sampler-checks}
leq_v <- matrix(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE,
                  FALSE, TRUE, TRUE,
                  FALSE, FALSE, TRUE), 3, 3, byrow = TRUE)
r <- sample_les(leq_v, 20000, 5000, 5, seed = 1)
stopifnot(abs(mean(r[, 1] < r[, 2]) - 0.5) < 0.03,
          all(r[, 3] == 2))
r <- sample_les(diag(3) == 1, 20000, 5000, 5, seed = 2)
stopifnot(all(abs(colMeans(r) - 1) < 0.04))
cat("Bubley-Dyer sampler checks passed\n")
```

*Result.* Both checks pass; the sampler produces uniform linear
extensions within Monte-Carlo tolerance.

## parsec setup check

```{r api-smoke-test}
# smallest non-trivial poset: two variables, two grades each
toy_profiles <- var2prof(varlen = c(2, 2))
print(toy_profiles$profiles)

toy_result <- evaluation(toy_profiles, threshold = "12")
print(round(toy_result$idn_f, 2))

# hand-computed: "11" below the threshold in both extensions -> 1;
# "12" is the threshold -> 1; "21" incomparable, below in 1 of 2 -> 0.5;
# "22" always above -> 0
expected <- c("11" = 1, "12" = 1, "21" = 0.5, "22" = 0)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(toy_result$idn_f[names(expected)]),
                           unname(expected), tolerance = 0.1)))
cat("parsec is set up correctly: matches the hand-computed values.\n")

# second orientation check, on rank_dist (used later for average ranks):
# measure the direction on this toy poset instead of assuming it
m_toy <- ncol(toy_result$rank_dist)
toy_avg_rank <- as.vector(toy_result$rank_dist %*% seq_len(m_toy))
names(toy_avg_rank) <- rownames(toy_result$rank_dist)
print(round(toy_avg_rank, 2))
rank_dist_needs_flip <- unname(toy_avg_rank["11"] > toy_avg_rank["22"])
cat("rank_dist orientation: rank 1 =",
    if (rank_dist_needs_flip) "MOST deprived -> flip needed before use\n"
    else "least deprived -> no flip needed\n")
```

*Result and decisions.* The toy case reveals that `parsec`'s `idn_f` is
the share of extensions ranking a profile *at or below* the threshold —
the mirror image of what this project calls identification. So on the
real data identification is `1 - idn_f`, and severity is `wea_rel` (not
`svr_rel`). The `rank_dist` orientation is likewise *measured* here, not
assumed, and the measured flag drives the average ranks used in the
composite comparison. Both catches came from this toy test, not from
guessing.

## Poset construction and identification (parsec)

The next chunks apply `parsec` to the real Schema A grades: build the
distinct observed profiles, embed the threshold profile, compute the
poset's structure, then estimate identification and severity against
$\tau = (1, \dots, 1)$ — the profile of a country in the medium band on
every surviving dimension at once.

**Why** $\tau = (1, \dots, 1)$, stated in full. The threshold is an
explicitly *normative* choice, not a statistical one. The literature on
ordinal multidimensional deprivation (Fattore 2016; Alkire & Foster
2011) is explicit that the cutoff is a value judgment that must be
declared transparently and stress-tested — which is what the robustness
section does. Reading countries as "at distance from normative target
levels" mirrors the OECD's own distance-to-target methodology for the
SDGs. And identifying against a profile rather than an aggregate score
is what lets the poset avoid the compensability assumption embedded in
every composite index (Ravallion 2012; Decancq & Lugo 2013; OECD/JRC
Handbook 2008). Under Schema A, $\tau$ reads: *at the EU target
boundary, or inside the declared tolerance band, on all five fronts at
once* — dominated profiles are unambiguously acceptable, dominating
profiles unambiguously not, and the incomparable middle is measured
rather than assumed away.

```{r real-profiles}
# parsec wants grades starting at 1, not 0
grades_a_parsec <- grades_a %>% mutate(across(-iso3, ~ . + 1))

country_profile_label <- grades_a_parsec %>%
  select(-iso3) %>%
  apply(1, paste0, collapse = "")

# threshold label built from n_dims, never hard-coded
threshold_label <- paste(rep(2L, n_dims), collapse = "")

observed_profiles <- pop2prof(grades_a_parsec %>% select(-iso3))
cat(sprintf("Distinct profiles among the %d countries: %d\n",
            n_countries, nrow(observed_profiles$profiles)))

# add the threshold as ONE weight-0 phantom row. Never merge the full
# theoretical support (3^n_dims profiles) just to place tau: the sampler's
# chain length grows ~n^5 with the number of profiles
threshold_row <- as.data.frame(as.list(rep(2L, n_dims)))
names(threshold_row) <- names(grades_a_parsec %>% select(-iso3))
augmented_data <- bind_rows(grades_a_parsec %>% select(-iso3), threshold_row)
augmented_weights <- c(rep(1, nrow(grades_a_parsec)), 0)
all_profiles <- pop2prof(augmented_data, weights = augmented_weights)
cat("Profiles after adding the threshold (if new):", nrow(all_profiles$profiles), "\n")

stopifnot(threshold_label %in% rownames(all_profiles$profiles))
```

*Result.* On the reference run the 24 countries collapse to **18
distinct profiles** (ties: AUT–GBR–LTU; CHE–CZE–SVN; BEL–IRL; FRA–POL);
$\tau = 11111$ (parsec encoding `22222`) is not observed and enters as a
19th, weight-0 profile.

```{r poset-structure}
# structure on the REAL country profiles only (not the tau placeholder)
zeta <- getzeta(observed_profiles)
profile_heights <- heights(zeta)
cat("Poset height:", max(profile_heights), "\n")
profile_levels <- levels(zeta)
cat("Poset width:", max(table(profile_levels)), "\n")
incomparable <- incomp(zeta)
share_incomparable <- mean(incomparable[upper.tri(incomparable)])
cat("Share of incomparable profile pairs:", round(share_incomparable, 3), "\n")
```

*Result.* Height 6, width 5, and **56% of distinct profile pairs are
incomparable** (44% when counted over country pairs, since ties
concentrate in the comparable bottom). More than half of the profile
comparisons the data allows are refusals to compare — this is the
structural fact the whole project is about.

```{r identification}
result <- evaluation(all_profiles, threshold = threshold_label, error = 1e-3)

# flip idn_f (measured on the toy poset above, not assumed)
deprivation_idn <- 1 - result$idn_f
severity <- result$wea_rel

country_results <- tibble(
  iso3 = grades_a$iso3,
  profile = country_profile_label,
  idn = deprivation_idn[country_profile_label],
  severity = severity[country_profile_label]
) %>% arrange(desc(idn), desc(severity))

print(country_results, n = n_countries)

cat("\nCertainly deprived (idn = 1):\n")
print(country_results %>% filter(idn == 1) %>% pull(iso3))
```

*Result.* Five countries are **certainly deprived** — their profiles
dominate $\tau$, so they rank above it in *every* admissible ranking:
**Spain, Italy, Austria, Lithuania, United Kingdom** (AUT, GBR and LTU
share one profile). Severity separates them: Spain (\~0.46) and Italy
(\~0.41) are far past the boundary; the AUT/GBR/LTU profile (\~0.20)
just past. Norway (\~0.95), Greece (\~0.91) and Sweden (\~0.90) are
near-certain but saved from certainty by a single good dimension each.
Nine countries have idn = 0.

## Scratch vs parsec cross-check

The same Schema A grades now go through the from-scratch toolbox, and
the two identification vectors are compared. This is the strongest
internal correctness check available: two independent implementations of
the same mathematics must agree.

```{r scratch-vs-parsec}
GA <- as.data.frame(grades_a %>% select(-iso3))
rownames(GA) <- grades_a$iso3
TAU <- rep(1L, n_dims)

scratch_results <- evaluate_scratch(GA, TAU)

cross_check <- country_results %>%
  select(iso3, idn_parsec = idn) %>%
  left_join(tibble(iso3 = rownames(scratch_results),
                   idn_scratch = scratch_results$idn),
            by = "iso3")
print(cross_check, n = n_countries)

rho_cross <- cor(cross_check$idn_scratch, cross_check$idn_parsec,
                 method = "spearman")
cat(sprintf("Cross-check scratch vs parsec — Spearman rho: %.4f\n", rho_cross))
stopifnot(rho_cross >= 0.95)   # in practice it should exceed 0.99
```

*Result.* On the reference run the agreement exceeds 0.99 — the
from-scratch implementation reproduces the reference one. This check
must hold on every re-run regardless of the data; if it ever fails, the
bug is in the code, not in the countries.

```{r idn-severity-plot, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=5.6}
pr <- country_results %>% arrange(idn, severity) %>%
  mutate(iso3 = factor(iso3, levels = iso3))
ggplot(pr) +
  geom_col(aes(idn, iso3), fill = "#1c7ed6", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(severity, iso3), fill = "#c92a2a", width = 0.45) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "identification (blue) and severity (red)", y = NULL,
       title = "Identification degree and severity — Schema A") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r hasse, fig.width=8.6, fig.height=6.4}
# Hasse diagram: nodes = distinct profiles (labelled with their countries),
# edges = cover relation, height = depth in the poset, tau in red
dp_h <- distinct_profiles(GA)
profiles_h <- rbind(dp_h$profiles, TAU)
members_h <- c(dp_h$members, list("_TAU_"))
leq_h <- leq_matrix(profiles_h)
strict_h <- leq_h & !diag(nrow(leq_h))
tau_idx_h <- nrow(profiles_h)
depth_h <- node_depths(strict_h)
cov_edges <- cover_relation(leq_h)

nodes <- data.frame(id = seq_len(nrow(profiles_h)), depth = depth_h,
                    key = apply(profiles_h, 1, paste, collapse = ""))
nodes$label <- sapply(members_h, function(mm)
  if (identical(mm, "_TAU_")) "tau" else paste(mm, collapse = ","))
nodes$is_tau <- seq_len(nrow(profiles_h)) == tau_idx_h
nodes <- nodes[order(nodes$depth, nodes$key), ]
nodes$x <- ave(seq_along(nodes$id), nodes$depth,
               FUN = function(k) (seq_along(k) - (length(k) + 1) / 2) * 1.35)
nodes <- nodes[order(nodes$id), ]
edges <- data.frame(x = nodes$x[cov_edges[, 1]],
                    y = nodes$depth[cov_edges[, 1]],
                    xend = nodes$x[cov_edges[, 2]],
                    yend = nodes$depth[cov_edges[, 2]])

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_label(data = nodes,
             aes(x, depth, label = label, fill = is_tau, colour = is_tau),
             size = 2.8, label.padding = unit(0.15, "lines"),
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#e7f5ff", `TRUE` = "#c92a2a")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "black", `TRUE` = "white")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "deprivation level (upward = worse)",
       title = "Hasse diagram — profile poset with threshold tau (red)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
```

*Result.* The diagram makes the certain set visible at a glance: the
five certainly-deprived countries occupy the nodes above the red $\tau$
node; the nine idn-0 countries the nodes below it; everything else hangs
beside it, incomparable.

## Composite index comparison

The alternative the poset argues against is now built fairly and simply:
min-max normalise the five oriented indicators, average them, rank. Any
divergence between this ranking and the poset's is then attributable to
the aggregation logic, not to exotic modelling.

```{r composite}
normalised <- as.data.frame(lapply(indicator_values,
                                   function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))))
composite_score <- rowMeans(normalised)

# poset average rank from rank_dist, flipped only if the toy-poset
# measurement said so
rownames(result$rank_dist) <- rownames(all_profiles$profiles)
m_real <- ncol(result$rank_dist)
poset_avg_rank_by_profile <- as.vector(result$rank_dist %*% seq_len(m_real))
if (rank_dist_needs_flip) {
  poset_avg_rank_by_profile <- m_real + 1 - poset_avg_rank_by_profile
}
names(poset_avg_rank_by_profile) <- rownames(result$rank_dist)
poset_avg_rank <- poset_avg_rank_by_profile[country_profile_label]
```

```{r composite-compare, fig.width=6, fig.height=5.6}
comparison <- tibble(
  iso3 = grades_a$iso3,
  idn = deprivation_idn[country_profile_label],
  severity = severity[country_profile_label],
  composite = composite_score,
  rank_poset = rank(poset_avg_rank),
  rank_composite = rank(composite_score)
) %>%
  mutate(rank_shift = rank_composite - rank_poset) %>%
  arrange(desc(idn))
print(comparison, n = n_countries)

rho_poset_composite <- cor(comparison$rank_poset, comparison$rank_composite,
                           method = "spearman")
cat("Spearman(poset rank, composite rank):", round(rho_poset_composite, 3), "\n")

ggplot(comparison, aes(rank_composite, rank_poset)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey80") +
  geom_point(colour = "#1c7ed6", size = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = iso3,
                colour = abs(rank_shift) >= 3,
                fontface = ifelse(abs(rank_shift) >= 3, "bold", "plain")),
            size = 2.7, nudge_x = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "black", `TRUE` = "#c92a2a")) +
  labs(x = "composite-index rank (1 = least deprived)",
       y = "poset average rank (1 = least deprived)",
       title = sprintf("Spearman rho = %.2f", rho_poset_composite)) +
  theme_minimal()

cat("\nLargest rank shifts (composite minus poset):\n")
print(comparison %>%
        arrange(desc(abs(rank_shift))) %>%
        select(iso3, idn, severity, rank_poset, rank_composite, rank_shift) %>%
        head(8))
```

*Result.* The two rankings correlate at **rho = 0.85**: the poset does
not produce noise. The disagreements are the point. **Austria** shifts 9
positions (9th for the composite, 18th for the poset) and the **UK** 8:
both are *certainly deprived* yet the average dilutes their critical
NEET configuration with good poverty and unemployment numbers.
**Denmark** shifts 9 positions the other way: the composite punishes its
high non-completion value, while the poset keeps it genuinely ambiguous
(idn \~0.47) because its NEET grade 0 blocks dominance. This is exactly
the class of information a single score erases.

## Robustness

Six checks, one per attackable choice: drop one indicator at a time
(jackknife on indicators), drop one country at a time (jackknife on
countries), replace Schema A with Schema B, change the number of grade
levels (3 vs 5), test whether the observed incomparability could arise
by chance (permutation test), and identify which dimensions block
certain identification (bottleneck analysis).

```{r jackknife-helper}
# repeated everywhere below: build profiles, embed threshold, evaluate.
# Mirrors exactly the main Schema A steps
identify_countries <- function(grades_tbl, threshold_grades) {
  parsec_grades <- grades_tbl %>% mutate(across(-iso3, ~ . + 1))
  label <- parsec_grades %>% select(-iso3) %>% apply(1, paste0, collapse = "")
  threshold_label <- paste0(threshold_grades + 1, collapse = "")
  threshold_row <- as.data.frame(as.list(threshold_grades + 1))
  names(threshold_row) <- names(parsec_grades %>% select(-iso3))
  augmented <- bind_rows(parsec_grades %>% select(-iso3), threshold_row)
  weights <- c(rep(1, nrow(parsec_grades)), 0)
  profiles <- pop2prof(augmented, weights = weights)
  stopifnot(threshold_label %in% rownames(profiles$profiles))
  res <- evaluation(profiles, threshold = threshold_label, error = 1e-3)
  idn <- 1 - res$idn_f
  tibble(iso3 = grades_tbl$iso3, idn = as.numeric(idn[label]))
}
```

```{r jackknife}
indicator_names <- setdiff(names(grades_a), "iso3")

jackknife_results <- lapply(indicator_names, function(drop_col) {
  keep_cols <- c("iso3", setdiff(indicator_names, drop_col))
  reduced_grades <- grades_a[keep_cols]
  reduced_tau <- rep(1L, length(keep_cols) - 1)
  identify_countries(reduced_grades, reduced_tau) %>%
    rename(!!paste0("idn_no_", drop_col) := idn)
}) %>% reduce(left_join, by = "iso3")

print(jackknife_results, n = n_countries)
write_csv(jackknife_results, "idea5_jackknife_idn_R.csv")

idn_cols <- setdiff(names(jackknife_results), "iso3")
jackknife_range <- jackknife_results %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(jk_min = min(c_across(all_of(idn_cols))),
         jk_max = max(c_across(all_of(idn_cols)))) %>%
  ungroup()
cat("\nCountries whose identification flips across jackknife folds:\n")
print(jackknife_range %>% filter(jk_min < 0.5, jk_max > 0.5) %>%
        select(iso3, jk_min, jk_max))
```

*Result.* The certain core is solid: the five idn-1 countries stay at 1
in every fold, and the nine idn-0 countries stay at 0. The middle is
honest about its fragility: eight countries (DNK, DEU, EST, FIN, HUN,
PRT, SVK, SWE) cross 0.5 in at least one fold — e.g. Hungary sits
exactly one dimension (poverty) below $\tau$, so dropping poverty sends
it to 1 and dropping its worst dimension sends it to 0. With five
dimensions, each fold removes 20% of the information; wide ranges in the
ambiguous middle are the expected behaviour, not a defect.

```{r jackknife-countries, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=5.6}
country_list <- grades_a$iso3
jk_countries <- lapply(country_list, function(drop_iso) {
  reduced <- grades_a %>% filter(iso3 != drop_iso)
  res <- identify_countries(reduced, rep(1L, n_dims))
  res %>% mutate(dropped = drop_iso)
}) %>% bind_rows()

jk_country_range <- jk_countries %>%
  group_by(iso3) %>%
  summarise(jk_min = min(idn), jk_max = max(idn), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(country_results %>% select(iso3, idn_full = idn), by = "iso3") %>%
  arrange(desc(idn_full))
print(jk_country_range, n = n_countries)

ggplot(jk_country_range %>%
         mutate(iso3 = factor(iso3, levels = iso3[order(idn_full)]))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = jk_min, xend = jk_max, y = iso3, yend = iso3),
               colour = "grey60", linewidth = 2.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(idn_full, iso3), colour = "#1c7ed6", size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "identification degree", y = NULL,
       title = "Country jackknife: idn range when one country is dropped") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Result.* Removing any single country moves the others' identification
by a few hundredths at most; no country's classification depends on the
presence of another. Certainty (idn = 1 or 0) is untouched by
construction — dominance relations against $\tau$ do not depend on the
rest of the sample.

```{r schema-b-compare, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=5.6}
result_b <- identify_countries(grades_b, rep(1L, n_dims))

schema_compare <- country_results %>%
  select(iso3, idn_a = idn) %>%
  left_join(result_b %>% rename(idn_b = idn), by = "iso3")

rho_a_b <- cor(schema_compare$idn_a, schema_compare$idn_b, method = "spearman")
cat("Spearman(idn Schema A, idn Schema B):", round(rho_a_b, 3), "\n")

cat("\nIdentified (idn > 0.5), Schema A:\n")
print(sort(schema_compare$iso3[schema_compare$idn_a > 0.5]))
cat("\nIdentified (idn > 0.5), Schema B:\n")
print(sort(schema_compare$iso3[schema_compare$idn_b > 0.5]))

schema_compare_long <- schema_compare %>%
  pivot_longer(c(idn_a, idn_b), names_to = "schema", values_to = "idn") %>%
  mutate(schema = recode(schema,
                         "idn_a" = "Schema A (policy)",
                         "idn_b" = "Schema B (terciles)"),
         iso3 = factor(iso3, levels = schema_compare$iso3[order(schema_compare$idn_a)]))
ggplot(schema_compare_long, aes(idn, iso3, colour = schema, shape = schema)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("Schema A (policy)" = "#1c7ed6",
                                       "Schema B (terciles)" = "#f08c00")) +
  scale_shape_manual(NULL, values = c(16, 15)) +
  labs(x = "identification degree", y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("Schema A vs B — Spearman rho = %.2f", rho_a_b)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

*Result.* Agreement is moderate (**rho \~0.60**) — by design, not by
failure: policy-anchored and relative cut-points answer different
questions. France is the textbook divergence: acceptable against EU
target bands (idn 0 under A) but among the worst against European
terciles (idn 1 under B) — mediocre on nearly everything, critical on
nothing. The certain Schema A core stays identified under B too.

```{r sensitivity-levels, fig.width=6, fig.height=4.4}
discretize_quintiles <- function(values) {
  breakpoints <- quantile(values, probs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2), na.rm = TRUE)
  breakpoints <- unique(breakpoints)
  as.integer(cut(values, breaks = breakpoints,
                 include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)) - 1L
}
grades_c <- oriented_matrix %>% mutate(across(-iso3, discretize_quintiles))
TAU_5 <- rep(2L, n_dims)
result_c <- identify_countries(grades_c, TAU_5)
cat("Identified (idn > 0.5), Schema C (quintiles):\n")
print(sort(result_c$iso3[result_c$idn > 0.5]))

inc_a <- incomparable_share(grades_a %>% select(-iso3))
inc_b <- incomparable_share(grades_b %>% select(-iso3))
inc_c <- incomparable_share(grades_c %>% select(-iso3))
comparison_levels <- tibble(
  schema = c("A — policy (3 levels)", "B — terciles (3 levels)",
             "C — quintiles (5 levels)"),
  levels = c(3, 3, 5),
  pct_incomparable = c(inc_a, inc_b, inc_c)
)
print(comparison_levels)

ggplot(comparison_levels, aes(schema, pct_incomparable, fill = schema)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1c7ed6", "#f08c00", "#2b8a3e")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% incomparable country pairs",
       title = "Incomparability grows with the number of levels") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Result.* Incomparability among country pairs: **44% (A) → 53% (B) → 67%
(C)**. Finer scales create more refusals to compare, as expected:
incomparability is partly a resolution choice, which is one more reason
to declare the discretisation openly.

```{r permutation-test, fig.width=6, fig.height=4.4}
# null model: permute each column independently — marginals preserved,
# associations between indicators destroyed
set.seed(42)
n_perm <- 1000
obs_inc <- incomparable_share(grades_a %>% select(-iso3))
perm_inc <- replicate(n_perm, {
  G_perm <- grades_a %>%
    select(-iso3) %>%
    mutate(across(everything(), sample))
  incomparable_share(G_perm)
})
p_value <- mean(perm_inc >= obs_inc)

cat(sprintf("Observed incomparability:          %.3f\n", obs_inc))
cat(sprintf("Mean under the null (permutation): %.3f ± %.3f\n",
            mean(perm_inc), sd(perm_inc)))
cat(sprintf("p-value (observed >= null):        %.3f\n", p_value))

if (p_value < 0.05) {
  cat("Incomparability significantly GREATER than chance: dimensions move independently.\n")
} else if (p_value > 0.95) {
  cat("Incomparability significantly SMALLER than chance: the poset is more\n")
  cat("ordered than random data — the dimensions are positively associated.\n")
} else {
  cat("Incomparability compatible with chance alone.\n")
}

tibble(perm = perm_inc) %>%
  ggplot(aes(perm)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_inc, colour = "#c92a2a", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = obs_inc + 0.01, y = n_perm / 20,
           label = sprintf("Observed\n%.3f", obs_inc),
           colour = "#c92a2a", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "% incomparable pairs (permutations)", y = "frequency",
       title = "Permutation test: is the incomparability structural?") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Result — read carefully, the sign matters.* Observed incomparability
(0.44) is significantly *below* the null mean (0.64, p ≈ 1 for the
"greater" direction). The poset is **more ordered than random data**:
the five dimensions are positively associated (deprivations cluster in
the same countries), which creates more dominance than independence
would. The honest reading is therefore *not* "the dimensions are
independent" — it is that even with this positive association, 44% of
country pairs remain incomparable: real structure *and* a large
irreducible zone where any complete ranking is an act of weighting.

```{r bottleneck, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=4.4}
# which dimensions sit BELOW tau for each country? Those grades are what
# saves a country from certain identification
tau_vec <- rep(1L, n_dims)
dim_names <- setdiff(names(grades_a), "iso3")

bottleneck_results <- grades_a %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    n_blocks = sum(c_across(all_of(dim_names)) < tau_vec),
    block_label = {
      blocks <- dim_names[c_across(all_of(dim_names)) < tau_vec]
      if (length(blocks) == 0) "none (certainly deprived)"
      else paste(blocks, collapse = ", ")
    }
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(country_results %>% select(iso3, idn), by = "iso3") %>%
  arrange(desc(idn)) %>%
  select(iso3, idn, n_blocks, block_label)
print(bottleneck_results, n = n_countries)

block_freq <- bottleneck_results %>%
  filter(n_blocks > 0) %>%
  separate_rows(block_label, sep = ", ") %>%
  count(block_label, sort = TRUE) %>%
  rename(dimension = block_label, n_blocking = n)
cat("\nDimensions blocking dominance (number of countries each):\n")
print(block_freq)

ggplot(block_freq, aes(reorder(dimension, n_blocking), n_blocking)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1c7ed6", alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "countries where this dimension blocks dominance",
       title = "Bottleneck analysis: what prevents certain identification?") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Result.* NEET blocks dominance most often (13 countries have grade 0 on
it), followed by low completion (11) and poverty (9); `lowskill_math`
blocks only once (Estonia) — because almost nobody meets the EU maths
target, that dimension rarely saves anyone. Norway, Greece and Sweden
illustrate the mechanism: each is kept off certainty by exactly one
grade-0 dimension.

# Limits that hold regardless of the exact numbers

The sample is "Europe", not the OECD, by construction (the cut-points
anchor to EU policy). Reference years are not aligned across indicators
(PISA 2022, Findex 2021, labour data 2023–24; documented cell by cell),
and the four Eurostat-substituted `low_completion` cells are a different
measurement concept from the OECD cells in the same column — logged
individually, with the orientation compensation, in
`cells_from_eurostat`. Age brackets differ across indicators (15–24,
18–25, 15-year-olds). The poverty line is nationally relative, so high
Nordic values reflect within-country relative disadvantage, not low
absolute living standards. `low_completion` borrows an early-leaver
target as its cut anchor while measuring non-completion, making those
cuts stricter than the target they cite. And both $\tau$ and the Schema
A cut-points are normative choices — declared, referenced, and
stress-tested above, which is the method's honesty, not its weakness:
composite indices make equivalent choices implicitly, through weights
nobody defends.
